original_extraction.evidence_text:
Take twelve slow, deep breaths. For the first three breaths, focus on your breathing. For the next
three breaths, notice your breathing and also notice what thoughts are running through your mind.
(Whatever they are, just let them be.) For the next three breaths, notice your breathing and also scan
your body and notice what you feel. (Whatever you feel, just make room for it.) For the final three
breaths, as well as connecting with your breathing, connect with your environment. Notice what
you can see, hear, taste, touch and smell, as well as staying aware of your breathing. Ready? Put the
book down now and give it a go.
Ex

---

The idea of Breathing to Connect is to increase self-awareness, accept what you’re thinking and
feeling, and connect with where you are and what you’re doing. Once you’ve done this, you’re in
the best psychological space to take effective—that is, life-enhancing— action, if that should seem
like the thing to do right then.

---

Breathing to Connect doesn’t have to be exactly twelve breaths; you can shorten or lengthen the
exercise as you like. So from now on, instead of the Ten Deep Breaths technique (from Chapter 7),
start Breathing to Connect throughout the day. Practise it at traffic lights, while waiting in line,
before you get out of bed in the morning, during your lunchbreak, while your computer is booting
up, while you’re waiting for your husband to get ready to go out.

---

Try longer and shorter versions of the exercise. At traffic lights you might have time for only three
or four slow, deep breaths. In a slow-moving grocery line, you may have time for 30 or more. You
don’t have to keep an exact count or follow the order precisely as described above.

---

In particular, start Breathing to Connect whenever you’re stressed or whenever you realise you’re
all caught up in thoughts and feelings. In the midst of a tense situation, even one deep breath can
give you precious seconds to collect your wits.
generation_rules: Begin with focusing solely on breathing for initial breaths
Gradually incorporate noticing thoughts, bodily sensations, and environment
Allow flexibility in breath count and sequence based on context and time availability
pause_rules: Intersperse slow, deep breaths with mindful observation
Use even a single deep breath in tense situations to create a pause for regaining composure
original_extraction.psychological_function: Facilitate mindfulness by focusing attention sequentially on breathing, thoughts, bodily sensations, and sensory environment, promoting psychological presence and stress reduction.
repetition_rules: Practice multiple times daily, especially during stress or when caught up in thoughts and feelings
No strict count required; adapt breath number to situation
symbolic_elements: breathing as a means to connect with self and environment
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: Increase self-awareness, acceptance of thoughts and feelings, and connection with the present environment to enable effective, life-enhancing action.
voice_rules: Use gentle, guiding instructions encouraging non-judgmental observation ('just let them be', 'just make room for it')
Encourage self-directed practice throughout daily activities
